title: DNS, TCP & TLS Handshakes, HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3
objectives: Break down the round trips between typing a URL and the first byte
Compare connection setup costs of HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
Explain what multiplexing fixes and what it cannot
Use preconnect deliberately where a handshake is unavoidable
body:
Before the first byte of your page can arrive, the browser must translate the hostname (DNS), open a TCP connection (one round trip), and negotiate TLS 1.3 (one more round trip, two for the older TLS 1.2). Only then does the HTTP request fly. On a 60 ms RTT link, that is roughly 180 ms of pure setup before any application data moves.

## The problem
Your API moved to a new domain and every first request feels heavier, but the payload is tiny and the server is fast. The delay is not transfer time — it is connection setup, and you need to reason about it per protocol instead of shrugging at the network.

## Constraints
- DNS adds up to one RTT unless cached by the OS, the browser or a previous lookup.
- TCP needs a SYN/ACK exchange; TLS 1.3 needs one extra RTT, TLS 1.2 needs two.
- HTTP/1.1 allows one outstanding request per connection at a time, so browsers open up to six parallel connections, each paying setup.
- HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one connection, so only the first request pays the full handshake — but a lost TCP packet stalls all streams (head-of-line blocking).
- HTTP/3 runs QUIC over UDP: 1-RTT setup (0-RTT on reconnect), no TCP-level head-of-line blocking, and connections survive network switches.

## Options
For a critical third-party origin you cannot control, the browser can set up the connection early:

```html
<!-- warm DNS, TCP and TLS while the parser keeps working -->
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://api.example.com" crossorigin>
<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://static.example.com">
```

For request volume, the protocol is the lever: HTTP/1.1 spreads requests across six cold connections, HTTP/2 pays setup once and multiplexes, HTTP/3 does the same while tolerating loss and mobility better.

## Tradeoffs
Preconnect spends origin CPU and device radio time on a connection you might never use, so it belongs only on origins you are certain the page will hit soon. HTTP/2 concentrates risk in one connection: a single congested path can hurt every stream. HTTP/3 is the best transport story but still depends on middlebox support and mature server tooling on your edge.

## Decision
Reuse connections and keep them warm — keep-alive plus few origins beats any protocol tuning. Preconnect at most one or two critical origins per page. Prefer HTTP/2 as the baseline and enable HTTP/3 where your CDN supports it, especially for mobile audiences.

## Measure it
In the Network panel, read the waterfall: the *Stalled*, *DNS lookup*, *Initial connection* and *SSL* segments show exactly where setup time went, and the connection ID column shows whether requests reused a socket. Track TTFB per origin before and after any change.

## Best practices
- Keep the number of distinct origins small; every new origin repeats DNS, TCP and TLS.
- Serve over TLS 1.3 so the handshake costs one RTT, not two.
- Preconnect only origins needed for the critical render or first interaction.
- Prefer one multiplexed connection over six parallel HTTP/1.1 sockets.
- Measure TTFB and setup segments per origin, before and after changes.

## Common mistakes
- Adding dns-prefetch and preconnect for a dozen domains, wasting radio time on connections never used.
- Blaming payload size for a slow first request when the waterfall shows 300 ms of SSL setup.
- Assuming HTTP/2 fixes packet loss — TCP head-of-line blocking moves the stall, it does not remove it.
- Measuring handshake cost on a datacenter connection with 1 ms RTT and concluding it does not matter.
- Reopening a new connection per request in client code (no keep-alive) and paying setup on every call.

examples.name: preconnect.html
examples.code:
<!doctype html>
<html>
<head>
  <!-- Set up the API origin early: DNS + TCP + TLS happen in parallel
       with parsing instead of serially before the first fetch -->
  <link rel="preconnect" href="https://api.example.com" crossorigin>

  <!-- Cheaper hint: resolve DNS only, for an origin used a bit later -->
  <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://cdn.example.com">

  <!-- Note: crossorigin matters. A preconnect without it warms a
       different connection than a credentialed CORS fetch will use. -->
</head>
<body>
  <script type="module">
    // First call to this origin reuses the warm connection instead of
    // paying ~2 RTT of setup inline.
    fetch("https://api.example.com/v1/session", { credentials: "include" })
      .then((r) => r.json())
      .then((session) => console.log("ready", session.user))
  </script>
</body>
</html>

exercise.prompt: Estimate connection setup cost in round trips. Given a network RTT and a protocol, compute the setup cost before the first request: HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 pay DNS (1 RTT) + TCP (1 RTT) + TLS 1.3 (1 RTT); HTTP/3 pays DNS (1 RTT) + QUIC 1-RTT handshake (1 RTT). Render the setup cost in milliseconds for each protocol and a verdict naming the biggest saving.
hints: Map each protocol to its RTT count first, then multiply by the RTT.
HTTP/2 has the same connection setup as HTTP/1.1; multiplexing saves connections, not setup RTTs.
The verdict only needs the difference between h2 and h3 setup in ms.

questions.prompt: On a fresh connection with TLS 1.3, which sequence best describes the setup before the first HTTP request?
options: DNS lookup, TCP handshake, TLS handshake
TCP handshake only — DNS happens at the CDN
questions.explanation: The browser must resolve the name, establish the TCP connection, then negotiate TLS; only after all three can it send the HTTP request. TLS 1.3 fits its handshake into one RTT.

questions.prompt: What problem does HTTP/3 (QUIC) remove that HTTP/2 over TCP cannot?
options: Transport-level head-of-line blocking from TCP packet loss
questions.explanation: HTTP/2 multiplexes streams but they share one TCP byte stream, so a lost packet stalls all of them; QUIC tracks streams independently over UDP.
